title: Cloud Incident Response
summary: Cloud incident response is the set of prepared actions a team takes when a security event occurs in infrastructure a provider operates on the customer's behalf. The mechanics differ from on-premises work in three ways. The control plane is reached through provider APIs, so an attacker's actions appear as authenticated API calls rather than strange local processes. Volatile evidence such as instance memory disappears if an instance is terminated rather than stopped. And the provider holds logs, flow records and metadata that the customer cannot obtain in any other way. Response therefore leans on identity forensics, API audit trails and snapshotting before remediation. It shows up whenever a cloud account is compromised, a storage location is exposed, or a workload starts mining cryptocurrency. The usual mistake is treating a cloud instance like a laptop: engineers terminate the offending server to stop the bleeding, destroy the only copy of memory, and rebuild without ever revoking the long-lived access keys the attacker created outside that server.

beginner.definition: Cloud incident response is the plan and the steps you follow when something goes wrong in the cloud. The cloud means computers and storage that a company rents from a provider instead of owning. You still have to find the problem, stop it, clean it up, and write down what happened. The only difference is that most of your evidence sits in the provider's tools.
beginner.whyItMatters: When an attacker gets into a cloud account, the damage can spread in minutes. They can copy data, create new users, or start expensive computers you must pay for. If you have no plan, people panic and delete the machine that holds the clues. A clear plan tells everyone who to call and what to save first. It also keeps you inside the law, because some countries require you to report a breach quickly.
howItWorks: Prepare before anything happens: agree who leads, who can shut systems down, and how you reach them out of hours.
Detect the problem using provider alerts, unusual login reports, and billing spikes that appear without a known reason.
Preserve evidence first, by taking snapshots of disks and copying logs to a separate account before you change anything.
Contain the damage by disabling the stolen keys, isolating the affected network, and removing the attacker's new accounts.
Eradicate and recover by rebuilding clean systems from trusted images, then watching them closely for a few days.
Review the timeline afterwards and fix the weakness that let the attacker in, so the same path is closed.
beginner.example: Picture a fire drill in a block of flats that you rent rather than own. The landlord owns the building and the alarm panel, but you own everything inside your flat. When smoke appears, you cannot simply smash the alarm panel, because the landlord controls it. You call the building manager, who can open locked doors and show you the camera footage. At the same time you save your own photos and documents before water damages them. Cloud incident response works in the same way as this drill. The provider runs the building and gives you logs and snapshots. You decide what to save, what to switch off, and who to tell.
takeaways: Decide in advance who can switch off a system, because asking during an incident wastes the minutes that matter.
Copy logs and disk snapshots to a safe place before you delete anything, because deleting destroys the evidence.
Tell the provider early, since only they can see some logs and stop activity outside your account.

objectives: Explain what cloud incident response means and how it differs from responding to a physical server.
Describe the main phases of a cloud incident response process and what happens in each phase.
Identify the cloud evidence sources that must be preserved before remediation begins.
Outline how to prepare access, roles and contacts before an incident occurs.
Recognise common mistakes such as destroying instances before evidence is collected.
